result.summary: Pindar celebrates Theron of Akragas' Olympic chariot victory at a feast honouring the Dioskouroi. He tells how Herakles brought the olive from the land of the Hyperboreans to shade Olympia and founded the games, then praises Theron as reaching the limits of human achievement.

scenes.title: Editorial introduction
scenes.summary: Notes on the ode's occasion, the Theoxenia feast, and Theron's clan's devotion to the Twins.

scenes.title: The poet's debt to Theron
scenes.summary: Pindar declares he will honour Akragas and Theron with a new song, as Pisa and the olive crown demand.

scenes.title: Herakles fetches the olive
scenes.summary: Herakles founds the Olympic games and, remembering the trees seen in the land of the Hyperboreans while hunting the hind, brings the olive to bare Olympia.
scenes.stakes: Olympia's precinct is bare and exposed to the sun's rays.

scenes.title: Praise of Theron
scenes.summary: The Twins attend the feast; Pindar says Theron's glory comes from honouring them, and that he reaches the pillars of Herakles, beyond which none can go.

alias_notes.explanation: Greek name 'sons of Zeus' for Kastor and Polydeukes together.
Periphrasis for Artemis, who received Herakles.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable image of the limits of human knowledge and achievement beyond the pillars of Herakles.

analysis.text: The ode links Theron's victory to Herakles' founding of the games, giving the athlete mythic prestige and tying piety toward the Twins to success.
The Theoxenia was a feast in which gods were invited as guests, reflecting the Greek value of hospitality (xenia); Theron's clan cultivated this cult.

legacy.text: The olive wreath became the traditional prize at Olympia, and the myth gave the Games a sacred origin.

fun_facts.text: Pindar's 'Water is best' opening line of the Olympian Odes is one of his most quoted phrases; here it appears in sentence 17.

language_notes.text: The Theoxenia was a feast in which gods were invited as guests to a table set for them; here Theron hosts the Dioskouroi's fellow gods.
Komos was a joyful procession of revellers who sang in honour of a victor; its songs were the typical victory celebration.
"Feet that move in Dorian time" means the dance-steps and metre of Dorian musical mode, which suits the choral performance.
Pisa is the district containing Olympia; the name stands for the games and their sanctuary.
The Hyperboreans were a legendary people dwelling beyond the North Wind, favoured by Apollo. Ister is the Danube.
The lines describe a full moon at evening, the Moon's light facing the setting sun; the games were founded at full moon.
Herakles' labour for Eurystheus was to capture the golden-horned hind sacred to Artemis (Leto's daughter).
"Water the best" echoes a proverbial saying of the time; the pillars of Herakles mark the western limit of the known world.

context_notes.text: The Emmenidai were Theron's family, rulers of Akragas in Sicily; they claimed the Dioskouroi as patrons.
The olive crown was the sole prize at Olympia, cut from a sacred wild olive.
Herakles is called son of Amphitryon, his mortal stepfather; his true father was Zeus.
The Tyndaridai are the Dioskouroi, sons of Tyndareus, patrons of horsemen and of hospitality.

literary_notes.text: "Pale-gleaming glory of olive" turns the crown into glory itself, joining the physical prize to the victor's fame.
The Moon rides a golden car and lights the "eye of Even", giving heavenly bodies the actions of persons.
The bare ground seems "given over" to the sun's keen rays, as though the garden were exposed and defenseless.
Theron's deeds are said to reach the pillars of Herakles, exalting his achievement to the very edge of the world.
The terse general maxim about the unreachable beyond warns against excess and closes the ode with a note of limit.
